# `silk/geometry/matrix`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Square 3x3 and 4x4 matrices for projective and three-dimensional transforms.

## When to use
Use [`Matrix3`](#Matrix3) for a projective transform of a plane, such as a perspective-correct image warp:
a homography that `silk.geometry.affine.Affine2` cannot express. Use [`Matrix4`](#Matrix4) for transforms
in space, such as a CSS `matrix3d`, a `perspective`, or a 3D rotation, and to project those
transforms back onto a plane. Use `Affine2` for every transform of a plane that keeps parallel
lines parallel; it is smaller and cheaper.

## Details
A matrix is a `Copy` struct that holds its entries in the public array `values` in column-major
order: entry `(row, column)` is `values[column * size + row]`. That is the order of WGSL, GLSL,
and CSS `matrix3d`, so a matrix copies to a GPU uniform or from CSS as written. A matrix
multiplies a column vector: `left * right` applies `right` first, then `left`.

[`Matrix3.project`](#Matrix3.impl.project) and [`Matrix4.project`](#Matrix4.impl.project) divide by the homogeneous `w` coordinate and return
`None` where `w` is zero. [`Matrix3.transformHomogeneous`](#Matrix3.impl.transformHomogeneous) and [`Matrix4.transformHomogeneous`](#Matrix4.impl.transformHomogeneous)
return the coordinates before that division, for renderers that must clip against `w`.

## Examples
### Round-trip a point through a perspective
```silk
import silk.geometry.matrix { Matrix4 }
import silk.geometry.point { Point3 }
import silk.core.option { Option }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let camera = Matrix4<f64>.perspective(100.0) * Matrix4<f64>.rotationY(0.5)
  let inverse = match camera.inverse() {
    Option<Matrix4<f64>>.Some { value } => value
    Option<Matrix4<f64>>.None => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let point = Point3<f64>.new(10.0, 20.0, 5.0)
  let back = match (inverse * camera).project(point) {
    Option<Point3<f64>>.Some { value } => value
    Option<Point3<f64>>.None => {
      return 2
    }
  }
  if back.x < 9.999999 || back.x > 10.000001 || back.z < 4.999999 || back.z > 5.000001 {
    return 3
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `Matrix3` with `import silk.geometry.matrix { Matrix3 }`.

## `Matrix3`

```silk
pub struct Matrix3<T>
```

A 3x3 matrix of number type `T`, stored in column-major order.

### When to use

Use `Matrix3` for a projective transform of a plane (a homography). Use
`silk.geometry.affine.Affine2` when the transform keeps parallel lines parallel.

### Details

Entry `(row, column)` is `values[column * 3 + row]`. The matrix maps `(x, y)` through the
homogeneous vector `(x, y, 1)`: `project` divides the first two results by the third. `left *
right` applies `right` first. `&a == &b` compares all nine entries when `T: Equal`.

<a id="Matrix3.values"></a>

### Field `values`

```silk
pub values: [T; 9]
```

The nine entries in column-major order: entry `(row, column)` is `values[column * 3 + row]`.

### Method `toAffine`

```silk
pub fn toAffine(self: Self) -> Option<Affine2<T>>
```

Returns the affine transform of the matrix, or `None` when its last row is not `[0 0 1]`.

#### Details

A matrix whose last row is `[0 0 1]` keeps parallel lines parallel. Any other last row
describes a perspective, which `Affine2` cannot hold.

### Method `project`

```silk
pub fn project(self: Self, point: Point2<T>) -> Option<Point2<T>>
```

Returns `point` mapped through the matrix and divided by `w`, or `None` where `w` is zero.

#### Gotchas

projection. Use `transformHomogeneous` to test the sign of `w` first.

## `Matrix4`

```silk
pub struct Matrix4<T>
```

A 4x4 matrix of number type `T`, stored in column-major order.

### When to use

Use `Matrix4` for transforms in space, such as CSS `matrix3d`, `perspective`, and 3D rotations.
Use `silk.geometry.affine.Affine2` for a transform of a plane.

### Details

Entry `(row, column)` is `values[column * 4 + row]`, the order of CSS `matrix3d(...)` arguments
and of WGSL `mat4x4`. The matrix maps `(x, y, z)` through the homogeneous vector `(x, y, z, 1)`:
`project` divides the first three results by the fourth. `left * right` applies `right` first.
`&a == &b` compares all sixteen entries when `T: Equal`.

<a id="Matrix4.values"></a>

### Field `values`

```silk
pub values: [T; 16]
```

The sixteen entries in column-major order: entry `(row, column)` is `values[column * 4 +
row]`.

<a id="Matrix4.impl.fromAffine"></a>

### Associated function `fromAffine`

```silk
pub fn fromAffine(transform: Affine2<T>) -> Matrix4<T>
```

Returns the matrix of `transform` acting on x and y, with z unchanged.

#### Details

This is the CSS rule for a 2D transform in a 3D context: `matrix(a, b, c, d, e, f)` equals
`matrix3d(a, b, 0, 0, c, d, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, e, f, 0, 1)`.

<a id="Matrix4.impl.toAffine"></a>

### Method `toAffine`

```silk
pub fn toAffine(self: Self) -> Option<Affine2<T>>
```

Returns the affine transform of the matrix, or `None` when it is not a 2D transform.

#### Details

The result is `Some` exactly when the matrix leaves z and w alone, as CSS "is 2D" requires:
entries `(2, 0)`, `(3, 0)`, `(2, 1)`, `(3, 1)`, `(0, 2)`, `(1, 2)`, `(3, 2)`, and `(2, 3)` are
zero and entries `(2, 2)` and `(3, 3)` are one.


#### Details

clockwise in a y-down space such as CSS.

<a id="Matrix4.impl.perspective"></a>

### Associated function `perspective`

```silk
pub fn perspective(distance: T) -> Matrix4<T>
```

Returns the CSS `perspective(distance)` matrix: a viewer at `distance` along positive z.

#### Details

The matrix is the identity with entry `(3, 2)` set to `-1 / distance`, so a point at depth `z`
scales by `distance / (distance - z)` after `project`.

#### Gotchas

A zero `distance` divides by zero. CSS treats `perspective(0)` as no perspective; pass the
identity in that case.


Returns `point` mapped through the matrix and divided by `w`, or `None` where `w` is zero.

<a id="Matrix4.impl.projectPoint2"></a>

### Method `projectPoint2`

```silk
pub fn projectPoint2(self: Self, point: Point2<T>) -> Option<Point2<T>>
```

Returns the point of the plane `z = 0` mapped through the matrix, flattened onto the x-y
plane, or `None` where `w` is zero.

#### When to use

Use `projectPoint2` to draw a 2D element under a CSS 3D transform: the element lies in the
plane `z = 0`, and the screen shows the x and y of each projected point.

```silk
pub fn inverse(self: Self) -> Option<Matrix4<T>>
```

Returns the matrix that undoes `self`, or `None` when `self` has no finite inverse.

#### Details

The inverse is the adjugate divided by the determinant. `None` means the determinant is zero,
or that the inverse has an infinite or NaN entry, such as when an input entry is infinite or
NaN.
